title: The Ark Installed and David's Song of Thanks
summary: The ark is placed in David's tent in Jerusalem with offerings, and David blesses the people and gives every household food. He appoints Asaph and other Levites to lead continual praise, and the chapter records a psalm of thanksgiving calling Israel and the nations to remember God's covenant and worship him. Worship is organized in two places: Asaph's singers before the ark in Jerusalem, and Zadok's priests at the tabernacle in Gibeon.
story: The ark has arrived. After the failure of chapter 13 and the careful procession of chapter 15, God's throne-chest now rests in the city of David. This chapter shows what the ark's arrival is for: not a single celebration but a pattern of ongoing praise. David sets people in place to give thanks regularly, day by day. The long psalm at the center tells the whole story in miniature, from the promise to Abraham to the day when the LORD comes to judge the earth. In chapter 17 David will want to build a permanent house for the ark, and God will answer with a promise about David's own house.
historical:
The chapter reflects a period when Israel's worship was divided between two sites. The tabernacle made under Moses, with its bronze altar, stood at the high place of Gibeon, about six miles northwest of Jerusalem (verse 39; compare 1 Kings 3:4). The ark, which had once stood inside that tabernacle, was now in a separate tent in Jerusalem. David staffed both: sacrifices continued at Gibeon under Zadok, while Asaph led praise before the ark. The arrangement lasted until Solomon's temple brought ark and altar together again.

The psalm in verses 8-36 corresponds closely to three psalms in the book of Psalms: verses 8-22 match Psalm 105:1-15, verses 23-33 match most of Psalm 96, and verses 34-36 match Psalm 106:1 and 106:47-48. Scholars differ on the relation. Some think the Chronicler drew on psalms already in use in the second temple and combined them for this scene; others think a Davidic original lies behind both forms. Either way, the prayer in verse 35 to gather and deliver us from the nations would have spoken directly to the Chronicler's first readers, Jews living under Persian rule, many of them still scattered.
cultural:
Burnt offerings were wholly consumed on the altar as an act of dedication; peace offerings (sometimes called fellowship offerings) were shared, with part burned, part given to the priests, and part eaten by the worshipers in a meal before God. David's gift of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake to every man and woman extended that meal to the whole people. The king blessing the people in the LORD's name was a sign that his rule stood under God's.

The singers' work was not background music. In ancient Israel, to remember God's deeds out loud was itself worship and testimony. The psalm's instructions to give thanks, call on his name, make known his deeds, sing, glory, seek, and remember describe the Levites' daily task. The closing response, when all the people said Amen and praised the LORD, shows the congregation joining in. The gatekeepers mentioned in verses 38 and 42 guarded the entrances to the holy area and controlled access to it.
literary: The chapter is framed by narrative (verses 1-7 and 37-43) around a single long psalm (verses 8-36). The psalm moves in three stages. It begins with Israel remembering the covenant God made with Abraham and swore to Isaac, when the people were few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land (verses 8-22). It widens to the nations and the whole creation: Sing to the LORD, all the earth, and even the trees of the forest sing because the LORD is coming to judge the earth (verses 23-33). It closes with thanks, a plea, and a blessing (verses 34-36). The refrain His loving devotion endures forever (verse 34) recurs in verse 41 and becomes a signature line in Chronicles, sung again at the dedication of Solomon's temple.

outline.t: The ark installed, offerings made, the people fed
Asaph and the Levites appointed to praise
Remember the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
All the earth and all creation praise the LORD who reigns
Thanks, a plea for rescue, and a blessing
Worship arranged in Jerusalem and at Gibeon

doctrines.note: The psalm roots Israel's worship in the covenant He made with Abraham and confirmed to Jacob, the word He ordained for a thousand generations (verses 15-17). Praise remembers God's commitments, and that memory becomes hope for a people still waiting.

Verse 26 is blunt: all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens. The Hebrew plays on the word for gods (elohim) and a word for worthless things (elilim). The difference between the true God and the others is that he is maker, not made.

The psalm repeatedly faces outward: make known His deeds among the nations, declare His glory among the nations, ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations. Israel's praise was meant to be heard by the world.
Worship includes petition. The people who praise also cry, Save us, O God of our salvation (verse 35). Thanksgiving and lament belong together in Israel's prayer.

words.note: Yadah, to give thanks or confess. It means to acknowledge publicly what God is and has done, which is why the same verb can describe confessing sin in other passages. It opens the psalm (verse 8) and names the Levites' appointed work (verse 4).

Zakar, to remember. In Hebrew thought remembering is active, calling the past into the present so that it shapes action. Israel is told to remember God's wonders (verse 12) and His covenant forever (verse 15). The Levites were appointed to lead this remembering (verse 4).

Chesed, rendered loving devotion in the BSB. It is covenant love: loyal, generous kindness that keeps faith with a promised relationship. Other translations use steadfast love, lovingkindness, or mercy. The refrain that God's chesed endures forever became one of Israel's central confessions.

Berit, covenant, a binding relationship with promises and obligations. Here it refers to God's sworn commitment to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, including the promise of the land. The ark itself is called the ark of the covenant, tying the object in the tent to the promise in the song.

christ: The psalm's promises reach beyond David. It celebrates the covenant with Abraham, which the New Testament says finds its fulfillment in Christ, the offspring through whom the nations are blessed (Galatians 3). It summons all the nations to worship Israel's God, which the apostles saw coming true as the gospel went to the Gentiles. It announces that the LORD reigns and is coming to judge the earth, language the New Testament applies to the return of Christ. The prayer to gather and deliver us from the nations is answered in part in the return from exile and more fully, in Christian reading, in the gathering of God's scattered people through Christ. None of this was hidden in the psalm as a code; it is the wider story taking up the psalm's own hopes.
questions: David appointed people to give thanks regularly, not only on a special day. What would change if thanksgiving were a daily practice rather than an occasional feeling?
The psalm reminds Israel that they were once few in number and strangers in the land. How does remembering where you came from shape how you worship now?
Verse 26 says the gods of the nations are idols. What things today receive the kind of trust and praise that belong to God alone?
